sections.heading: Glossary term: Copernican Revolution
sections.body: The Copernican Revolution refers to the replacement of the geocentric (Earth-centered) model of visualizing the Solar System with a heliocentric (Sun-centered) model. The geocentric model was the consensus in European scientific views for close to two millennia, even though some believed in a heliocentric model. This shift provided a first step in the move towards a new model for the motions of planets, moons, stars, and other celestial objects in the sky that occurred over the following centuries. The geocentric model is still used for explaining concepts related to the celestial sphere. The Copernican Revolution is named after Nicolaus Copernicus, who in the 16th century described the heliocentric model in his seminal work De revolutionibus orbium coelestium. Although it is often claimed Immanuel Kant was the first to use the term Copernican Revolution, the accuracy of this claim is debated.

Glossary term: Copernican Revolution

Description: The Copernican Revolution refers to the replacement of the geocentric (Earth-centered) model of visualizing the Solar System with a heliocentric (Sun-centered) model. The geocentric model was the consensus in European scientific views for close to two millennia, even though some believed in a heliocentric model. This shift provided a first step in the move towards a new model for the motions of planets, moons, stars, and other celestial objects in the sky that occurred over the following centuries. The geocentric model is still used for explaining concepts related to the celestial sphere. The Copernican Revolution is named after Nicolaus Copernicus, who in the 16th century described the heliocentric model in his seminal work De revolutionibus orbium coelestium. Although it is often claimed Immanuel Kant was the first to use the term Copernican Revolution, the accuracy of this claim is debated.

Related Terms:

  • Celestial Sphere
  • Geocentric Model
  • Heliocentric Model
  • Copernican Principle


See this term in other languages

Term and definition status: This term and its definition have been approved by a research astronomer and a teacher

The OAE Multilingual Glossary is a project of the IAU Office of Astronomy for Education (OAE) in collaboration with the IAU Office of Astronomy Outreach (OAO). The terms and definitions were chosen, written and reviewed by a collective effort from the OAE, the OAE Centers and Nodes, the OAE National Astronomy Education Coordinators (NAECs) and other volunteers. You can find a full list of credits here. All glossary terms and their definitions are released under a Creative Commons CC BY-4.0 license and should be credited to "IAU OAE".

sections.body_ru: Коперниканская революция относится к замене геоцентрической (с центром на Земле) модели визуализации Солнечной системы гелиоцентрической (с центром на Солнце) моделью. Геоцентрическая модель была консенсусом в европейских научных взглядах почти два тысячелетия, хотя некоторые верили в гелиоцентрическую модель. Этот сдвиг стал первым шагом к новой модели движений планет, лун, звёзд и других небесных объектов на небе, которая возникла в последующие столетия. Геоцентрическая модель до сих пор используется для объяснения понятий, связанных с небесной сферой. Коперниканская революция названа в честь Николая Коперника, который в 16 веке описал гелиоцентрическую модель в своём основополагающем труде De revolutionibus orbium coelestium. Хотя часто утверждается, что Иммануил Кант был первым, кто использовал термин «Коперниканская революция», точность этого утверждения обсуждается.

Copernicus's heliocentric system

Caption: Sketch of Copernicus's heliocentric model of the Solar System, from his book "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the revolution of the heavenly spheres) published in 1543. Shown are the Sun as well as the orbits of Mercury, Venus, the Earth (itself orbited by the Moon), Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. The outermost circle represents the sphere of the stars. In this model, the Earth is not special – it is merely one planet, among several, orbiting the Sun. This was the first example for what is now known as the Copernican Principle: that our positions as observers in the universe is not special or privileged in any way. The shift from the geocentric to the heliocentric model of our universe is known as the Copernican revolution.

media.caption_en:
Sketch of Copernicus's heliocentric model of the Solar System, from his book "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the revolution of the heavenly spheres) published in 1543. Shown are the Sun as well as the orbits of Mercury, Venus, the Earth (itself orbited by the Moon), Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. The outermost circle represents the sphere of the stars.

In this model, the Earth is not special – it is merely one planet, among several, orbiting the Sun. This was the first example for what is now known as the Copernican Principle: that our positions as observers in the universe is not special or privileged in any way. The shift from the geocentric to the heliocentric model of our universe is known as the Copernican revolution.
media.caption_ru:
Набросок гелиоцентрической модели Солнечной системы Коперника из его книги "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (О вращении небесных сфер), опубликованной в 1543. Показаны Солнце, а также орбиты Меркурия, Венеры, Земли (вокруг которой обращается Луна), Марса, Юпитера и Сатурна. Самый внешний круг представляет сферу звёзд.

В этой модели Земля не является особенной – она всего лишь одна планета из нескольких, обращающихся вокруг Солнца. Это был первый пример того, что сейчас известно как принцип Коперника: наше положение как наблюдателей во Вселенной не является особенным или привилегированным каким-либо образом. Переход от геоцентрической к гелиоцентрической модели нашей Вселенной известен как коперниканская революция.
